# Tetrahedron edge unions: exact thin-tube coverage and its scope

Let S be a tetrahedron, with barycentric coordinates lambda_0,...,
lambda_3, and let H_i={lambda_i>=1/4} be its four canonical
centroid caps. This note proves a uniform bound for an ARBITRARY
union of excluded caps near a fixed edge. It also records an exact
geometric obstruction to assuming that every small excluded cap
has that localization.

## 1. An arbitrary thin-edge union has coverage at most 3/2

Let R be a union, finite or infinite, of strict halfspace traces

    a lambda_0+b lambda_1>c lambda_2+d lambda_3,
    a,b>=0, a+b>0, c,d>0.

Assume the WHOLE union satisfies

    R subset {lambda_2+lambda_3<=1/4}.              (1)

Then

    sum_(i=0)^3 |R intersect H_i| <=(3/2)|R|
                                      <(27/16)|R| (2)

when R has positive volume. No number-of-cuts or disjointness
assumption is made. All union sets are relatively open in S and
are therefore measurable.

Use projective edge coordinates

    lambda_0=(1-t)/(1+y+z), lambda_1=t/(1+y+z),
    lambda_2=y/(1+y+z), lambda_3=z/(1+y+z),
    0<=t<=1, y,z>=0.

The volume Jacobian, apart from the fixed affine-coordinate factor
of S, is (1+y+z)^(-4). Each excluded cap becomes

    c y+d z<a+(b-a)t.

In polar coordinates y=r cos(theta), z=r sin(theta), 0<=theta<=pi/2,
the radial extent of the union is

    R_theta(t)=sup_caps [a+(b-a)t]/[c cos(theta)+d sin(theta)].

This is a nonnegative convex function of t (values zero at an endpoint
are harmless). The use of a supremum changes neither the radial
integral nor any volume if an endpoint is excluded. Condition (1)
gives k R_theta(t)<=1/3, where k=cos(theta)+sin(theta).

For fixed k, define

    W_k(r)=integral_0^r s/(1+k s)^4 ds.

It is increasing and

    W_k''(r)=(1-3k r)/(1+k r)^5>=0

on the whole relevant range. Thus W_k(R_theta(t)) is convex in t,
and so is the actual longitudinal volume density

    f(t)=integral_0^(pi/2) W_k(R_theta(t)) dtheta.   (3)

All functions are measurable: R_theta is a supremum of continuous
functions, and the uniformly bounded radial range makes the integrals
finite. The conclusion follows directly from pointwise convexity,
without differentiating the supremum.

For every nonnegative convex f on [0,1],

    integral_(1/4)^(3/4) f <=(1/2) integral_0^1 f.  (4)

Indeed g(t)=f(t)+f(1-t) is convex and symmetric, hence nonincreasing
on [0,1/2]. Its integral on [1/4,1/2] is no larger than its
integral on [0,1/4], proving (4).

On R, the caps H_2,H_3 have zero volume by (1). Further,
H_0 implies t<=3/4 and H_1 implies t>=1/4. Their simultaneous
coverage is therefore at most 1+1_{[1/4,3/4]}(t). Integration
against (3), followed by (4), proves (2). The margin is exact:
27/16-3/2=3/16.

This is an actual weighted longitudinal convexity statement. It
does not replace the volume Jacobian by a constant or infer it
from convexity of an unweighted transverse area.

## 2. Small missing volume need not imply thin-edge localization

In the standard tetrahedron, put 0<epsilon<=1/100 and

    Q_epsilon=S intersect
        {epsilon(lambda_0+lambda_1-2lambda_2)<=lambda_3},
    R_epsilon=S\Q_epsilon.

All FOUR facet centroids of S lie in Q_epsilon; the centroid of
facet lambda_3=0 lies exactly on the new plane. Also

    dist_H,barycentric-infinity(Q_epsilon,S)<=epsilon.

To verify the distance, write F=epsilon(lambda_0+lambda_1-2lambda_2)
-lambda_3. For any excluded x, F(x)<=epsilon and F(v_3)=-1.
The point (x+F(x)v_3)/(1+F(x)) belongs to the new plane and is
within epsilon in barycentric infinity norm of x.

Nevertheless the fixed point with barycentrics (.36,.36,.28,0)
belongs to R_epsilon for EVERY epsilon>0. It lies in three
canonical centroid caps and has lambda_2+lambda_3>1/4. Thus the
small-volume or near-simplex assumptions do not imply (1).
The actual missing set is a thin FACET layer reaching a finite
distance in one of the transverse directions to edge 01.

Here its total relative volume and its nonzero canonical losses
are exactly

    tau=|R_epsilon|/|S|
        =epsilon(5epsilon+8)/[9(1+epsilon)^2],
    |R_epsilon intersect H_0|/|S|
      =|R_epsilon intersect H_1|/|S|
        =epsilon(11epsilon+23)/[36(1+epsilon)^2],
    |R_epsilon intersect H_2|/|S|
        =epsilon(23epsilon+26)/[576(1+epsilon)^2],
    |R_epsilon intersect H_3|=0.                   (5)

For one elementary way to compute (5), a tetrahedron affine margin
with two equal positive vertex values a and negative values c,d
has positive-cap volume fraction

    [3a^2(a-c)(a-d)-a^3(2a-c-d)]/[(a-c)^2(a-d)^2]. (6)

Formula (6) follows by integrating the linear slices of the cap,
without requiring a repeated-knot convention. In the projective
coordinates of Section 1 its fraction is six times

    integral_(y=0)^(a/(-c)) integral_(z=0)^((a+c y)/(-d))
                               (1+y+z)^(-4) dz dy.

The elementary antiderivative gives (6); equal negative values
follow either by the same integral or continuity. For a canonical
trace lambda_i>=1/4, first apply the affine
copy (1/4)v_i+(3/4)S, multiply its volume by 27/64, and use its
four transformed margin values in (6).

The ratio in (2) for this wider example is

    sum_i |R_epsilon intersect H_i|/|R_epsilon|
      =3(125epsilon+254)/[64(5epsilon+8)]<3/2,

since the gap from 3/2 equals
3(35epsilon+2)/[64(5epsilon+8)]>0. Its limit is 381/256.
Thus this example refutes the GEOMETRIC thin-edge implication,
not the desired coverage inequality. Applying Section 1 to a
general near-tetrahedron body would require a further argument
for these one-short-transverse facet layers and for overlap among
different edge groupings. Neither step is assumed here.
